source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Encouraging deep hip flexion well beyond 90 degrees as part of the client's early post-operative recovery exercises","B":"Avoiding excessive hip flexion, internal rotation, and adduction, per the specific surgical approach and surgeon's recommendations","C":"Fairly few specific movement precautions actually being needed following a total hip replacement surgical procedure","D":"Encouraging the client to cross their legs while seated during the early weeks of their post-operative recovery"}}
source_row.rationale: Post-total hip replacement precautions to reduce dislocation risk may include avoiding excessive hip flexion, internal rotation, and adduction (such as crossing the legs), with specific precautions varying somewhat based on the surgical approach used and the individual surgeon's recommendations.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Hip Replacement Precautions
source_row.source_detail: Movement Precautions to Prevent Dislocation

source_row.stem: A nurse implements enhanced fall prevention measures for a client recovering from orthopedic surgery. These measures are particularly important because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Standard fall precautions generally requiring fairly little modification at all for this particular post-surgical client population","B":"Clients recovering from orthopedic surgery generally carrying fairly little added risk of experiencing a fall during their recovery","C":"Post-surgical pain, mobility limitations, and sometimes medication effects (such as from opioids) can increase fall risk during this recovery period","D":"Fall prevention being relevant mainly during the first 24 hours after surgery, rather than throughout the client's entire recovery period"}}
source_row.rationale: Enhanced fall prevention measures are particularly important after orthopedic surgery because post-surgical pain, mobility limitations from the procedure itself, and sometimes medication effects (such as sedation from opioid pain management) can increase fall risk throughout the recovery period, not just the immediate post-operative hours.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Fall Prevention After Orthopedic Surgery
source_row.source_detail: Fall Risk Factors in Post-Surgical Orthopedic Patients

source_row.stem: An orthopedic nurse's role typically involves:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A role fairly similar to a general medical-surgical staff nurse position, without much specialized orthopedic-specific focus built into it","B":"Mostly administrative scheduling tasks for the unit, with fairly little direct clinical involvement in the client's overall recovery","C":"Fairly little involvement in coordinating the client's ongoing mobility progress or their broader rehabilitation planning process","D":"Providing specialized care for clients with musculoskeletal conditions, including pre- and post-operative care, casting/traction management, and patient education"}}
source_row.rationale: An orthopedic nurse's role typically involves providing specialized care for clients with musculoskeletal conditions, including pre- and post-operative surgical care, casting/traction management, and patient education, along with coordination of mobility and rehabilitation needs.
source_row.source_name: National Association of Orthopaedic Nurses — Scope of Practice
source_row.source_detail: Scope of Orthopedic Nursing Role

source_row.stem: A nurse coordinates physical therapy services for a client recovering from orthopedic surgery. This coordination is important because physical therapy:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Supports functional recovery through structured exercise, mobility training, and strength building, an essential component of comprehensive orthopedic care","B":"Applying mainly to clients undergoing joint replacement surgery specifically, rather than to orthopedic recovery more broadly across the board","C":"Carrying fairly little established role much in helping clients recover physical function after undergoing orthopedic surgery","D":"Generally being postponed by the care team until the client reports being largely free of any pain whatsoever during their recovery"}}
source_row.rationale: Physical therapy supports functional recovery through structured exercise, mobility training, and strength building, an essential component of comprehensive orthopedic care applicable across a range of orthopedic conditions and surgeries, typically initiated relatively early in the recovery process rather than only once pain is completely resolved.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Physical Therapy in Orthopedic Recovery
source_row.source_detail: Role of Physical Therapy Coordination

source_row.stem: A nurse coordinates occupational therapy services for a client with significant functional limitations following an orthopedic injury. Occupational therapy focuses on:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Carrying fairly little established role in supporting clients who are recovering from an orthopedic injury of this particular kind","B":"Supporting the client's ability to perform activities of daily living and adapt to functional changes, complementing the work of physical therapy","C":"Applying mainly to clients with upper extremity injuries specifically, rather than to orthopedic clients more broadly across the board","D":"Focusing only on physical strength training, in essentially the same way that physical therapy already does for the client"}}
source_row.rationale: Occupational therapy focuses on supporting a client's ability to perform activities of daily living (such as dressing, bathing, and other functional tasks) and adapt to functional changes, complementing the more mobility/strength-focused work of physical therapy, applicable to both upper and lower extremity orthopedic conditions.
source_row.source_name: AOTA — Occupational Therapy Role in Orthopedic Recovery
source_row.source_detail: Distinction and Value of Occupational Therapy

source_row.stem: A nurse begins discharge planning early in a client's hospital stay following joint replacement surgery. Comprehensive discharge planning typically addresses:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly few specific components actually being included beyond the standard discharge instructions given to any surgical client","B":"Ongoing rehabilitation needs, home safety, mobility equipment needs, and pain management planning","C":"A single, generic discharge plan applied in essentially the same way to every joint replacement client, regardless of individual needs","D":"Mainly the discharge date itself, with comparatively little else built into the overall planning process"}}
source_row.rationale: Comprehensive discharge planning after joint replacement surgery typically addresses ongoing rehabilitation needs, home safety considerations, mobility equipment needs, and pain management planning, individualized to the client's specific functional status, home environment, and support system.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Joint Replacement Discharge Planning Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Components of Comprehensive Discharge Planning

source_row.stem: A nurse refers a client to home health services following discharge after orthopedic surgery. This referral may be appropriate when the client:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Being discharged instead to a skilled nursing facility, rather than needing home health services specifically arranged","B":"Having fairly few functional limitations and a fairly high level of independence noted at the time of discharge home","C":"Requires ongoing skilled nursing or therapy services, or has significant mobility limitations requiring support to safely manage at home","D":"Having already fully completed every one of their rehabilitation goals well before the referral is even being considered"}}
source_row.rationale: Home health referral after orthopedic surgery may be appropriate when a client requires ongoing skilled nursing or therapy services, or has significant mobility limitations requiring support to safely manage at home, bridging the gap between hospital discharge and full independent recovery.
source_row.source_name: CMS — Home Health Eligibility Criteria
source_row.source_detail: Appropriate Home Health Referral Criteria

source_row.stem: A nurse coordinates durable medical equipment (DME), such as a walker or raised toilet seat, for a client being discharged after hip surgery. This equipment coordination supports:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Offering fairly little meaningful benefit to the client's recovery once they return home from the hospital","B":"Safe mobility and independence with activities of daily living during the recovery period at home","C":"Equipment needs being considered essentially identical for every client, without much regard for individual assessment findings","D":"A process generally lacking any established insurance coverage considerations worth discussing with the client"}}
source_row.rationale: DME coordination, such as arranging a walker or raised toilet seat, supports safe mobility and independence with activities of daily living during the recovery period at home, individualized based on the client's specific functional needs and home environment assessment.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — DME Coordination After Orthopedic Surgery
source_row.source_detail: Purpose of Durable Medical Equipment Coordination

source_row.stem: A nurse cares for a client with a work-related orthopedic injury involved in a workers' compensation claim. The nurse should understand that this process typically involves:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A process entirely separate from the client's standard clinical care, with fairly little nursing involvement generally expected in most facilities","B":"Fairly few specific documentation considerations actually going beyond what standard clinical care would already typically require of the nurse","C":"Documentation requirements considered essentially identical to those required for any other routine clinical situation the nurse might encounter","D":"Careful, objective documentation of the injury, treatment, and functional status, given the role this information plays in the workers' compensation claims process"}}
source_row.rationale: Workers' compensation cases typically involve careful, objective documentation of the injury, treatment, and functional status, given the significant role this clinical information plays in the workers' compensation claims process, requiring particular attention to thorough, accurate documentation.
source_row.source_name: Standard Occupational Health Nursing References — Workers' Compensation Documentation
source_row.source_detail: Documentation Considerations in Workers' Compensation Cases

source_row.stem: A nurse supports a client undergoing a formal disability evaluation related to a significant orthopedic injury. This process typically involves:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A comprehensive functional assessment, often using standardized criteria, to determine the extent and impact of the client's limitations","B":"Carrying fairly little established relationship to the client's actual functional status or day-to-day limitations experienced","C":"A process completed entirely by the nurse working alone, with fairly little involvement expected from any other provider","D":"A fairly brief, informal assessment without much in the way of standardized components actually built into it"}}
source_row.rationale: Formal disability evaluation typically involves a comprehensive functional assessment, often using standardized criteria, to determine the extent and impact of the client's limitations on their ability to work or perform daily activities, generally involving multiple providers and specific documentation requirements.
source_row.source_name: Standard Occupational Health References — Disability Evaluation Process
source_row.source_detail: Components of Formal Disability Evaluation

source_row.stem: A nurse explains osteoporosis pathophysiology to a client. This condition is characterized by:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A condition generally considered to carry fairly little established relationship to a client's overall fracture risk","B":"Increased bone density with fairly little corresponding fracture risk for the affected client","C":"A condition affecting mainly the skin, with comparatively little involvement of the underlying bone tissue","D":"Reduced bone density and quality, resulting in bone that is more fragile and susceptible to fracture, often from minimal trauma"}}
source_row.rationale: Osteoporosis is characterized by reduced bone density and quality, resulting in bone that is more fragile and susceptible to fracture, often from minimal trauma that would not typically cause a fracture in bone with normal density.
source_row.source_name: National Osteoporosis Foundation — Osteoporosis Pathophysiology
source_row.source_detail: Characteristic Features of Osteoporosis

source_row.stem: A nurse differentiates osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis based on clinical presentation. Rheumatoid arthritis is more typically associated with:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A condition that essentially never produces any noticeable joint symptoms in the clients who happen to have it","B":"Symmetric joint involvement, significant morning stiffness lasting more than an hour, and systemic inflammatory features","C":"Presenting in a way that is essentially indistinguishable from osteoarthritis, without any features that set the two apart","D":"Pain that tends to worsen with activity and ease with rest, typically affecting weight-bearing joints in an asymmetric pattern"}}
source_row.rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis is more typically associated with symmetric joint involvement, significant morning stiffness lasting more than an hour, and systemic inflammatory features, distinct from osteoarthritis, which more typically presents with asymmetric, activity-related pain that improves with rest and shorter morning stiffness.
source_row.source_name: American College of Rheumatology — RA vs. OA Clinical Distinction
source_row.source_detail: Key Differentiating Features of RA

source_row.stem: A client with a recent long bone fracture develops sudden dyspnea, confusion, and a petechial rash over the chest and axillae within 48 hours of injury. The nurse should suspect:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An improvement in the client's overall neurological function noted within 48 hours of the fracture occurring","B":"A fairly simple allergic reaction to a medication, since a petechial rash is thought to commonly reflect this simpler cause","C":"Fat embolism syndrome, a serious complication of long bone fracture requiring immediate evaluation and supportive management","D":"A fairly ordinary, expected finding after a long bone fracture that would not typically call for urgent action"}}
source_row.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, confusion, and a petechial rash (classically distributed over the chest, axillae, and conjunctivae) developing within 24-72 hours of a long bone fracture are classic signs of fat embolism syndrome, a serious complication requiring immediate evaluation and primarily supportive management; the full classic triad of respiratory, neurological, and dermatological findings is not always present.
source_row.source_name: PMC — Fat Embolism Syndrome Clinical Recognition
source_row.source_detail: Classic Triad and Timing of Fat Embolism Syndrome

source_row.stem: A nurse explains the general stages of fracture healing to a client. This process generally progresses through:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A process generally considered unrelated to blood supply or to the underlying biological mechanisms of healing","B":"Essentially identical healing timelines for every fracture, regardless of the bone involved or the type of break","C":"Sequential stages, including hematoma formation, soft callus formation, hard callus formation, and remodeling","D":"A single, essentially instantaneous stage of healing, without any meaningful progression occurring over time"}}
source_row.rationale: Fracture healing generally progresses through sequential stages, including hematoma formation, soft callus formation, hard callus formation, and remodeling, a biological process influenced by factors such as blood supply, fracture location, and individual patient factors, with healing time varying accordingly.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Fracture Healing Process
source_row.source_detail: Sequential Stages of Fracture Healing

source_row.stem: A client with a femoral neck fracture is at risk for avascular necrosis of the femoral head. This complication results from:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Excess blood flow to the affected bone","B":"A condition unrelated to blood supply","C":"Disruption of blood supply to the bone, leading to bone tissue death","D":"A normal, expected part of fracture healing requiring no concern"}}
source_row.rationale: Avascular necrosis results from disruption of blood supply to the bone, leading to bone tissue death, a recognized risk following certain fractures (such as femoral neck fractures) where the blood supply to a specific bone segment can be compromised by the injury.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Avascular Necrosis Following Fracture
source_row.source_detail: Pathophysiology of Avascular Necrosis

source_row.stem: A client reports leg pain and numbness that worsens with walking and standing, but improves with sitting or leaning forward. The nurse should suspect:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An improvement in the client's overall neurological function that develops the longer they continue walking and standing","B":"Spinal stenosis, narrowing of the spinal canal that can compress nerve structures, particularly during extension-related positions like standing","C":"An unrelated vascular condition, with fairly little connection to how the client's symptoms actually change with body positioning","D":"A fairly ordinary, expected finding that would not typically call for any further clinical evaluation or workup"}}
source_row.rationale: Leg pain and numbness that worsens with walking/standing and improves with sitting or leaning forward (neurogenic claudication) is a classic presentation of spinal stenosis, narrowing of the spinal canal that compresses nerve structures more significantly during extension-related positions like standing.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Spinal Stenosis Clinical Presentation
source_row.source_detail: Recognition of Neurogenic Claudication in Spinal Stenosis

source_row.stem: A client presents with sudden low back pain radiating down one leg, following a specific dermatomal pattern, with associated numbness. The nurse should suspect:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An unrelated cardiac condition, since radiating leg pain is thought to commonly stem from this simpler alternative cause","B":"A herniated intervertebral disc, potentially compressing a spinal nerve root, causing the radiating pain pattern (radiculopathy)","C":"A fairly ordinary, expected finding that would not typically call for any further clinical evaluation","D":"An improvement in the client's overall neurological function reflected by this sudden new symptom pattern"}}
source_row.rationale: Sudden low back pain radiating down one leg in a specific dermatomal pattern with associated numbness is classic for a herniated intervertebral disc compressing a spinal nerve root, causing radiculopathy (nerve root-related pain and sensory changes following the specific dermatome of the affected nerve).
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Herniated Disc Clinical Presentation
source_row.source_detail: Recognition of Disc-Related Radiculopathy

source_row.stem: A client following lower extremity amputation reports pain that feels like it is coming from the amputated limb. The nurse should recognize this as:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A fairly ordinary finding that would be expected to fully resolve within 24 hours in essentially every affected client","B":"An imaginary symptom without any real physiological basis, not warranting any formal acknowledgment or assessment","C":"A sign of a surgical complication requiring emergency intervention in essentially every case where it is reported","D":"Phantom limb pain, a recognized and real phenomenon related to changes in the nervous system, requiring appropriate assessment and management"}}
source_row.rationale: Phantom limb pain is a recognized and real phenomenon, related to changes in the nervous system following amputation (not merely psychological), requiring appropriate assessment and management, including validation of the client's experience since this pain is genuinely felt despite the limb's absence.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Phantom Limb Pain Recognition and Management
source_row.source_detail: Physiological Basis and Validation of Phantom Limb Pain

source_row.stem: A nurse explains the purpose of a DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) scan to a client being evaluated for osteoporosis. This test measures:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The client's overall muscle strength, rather than any measure related to their bone health","B":"The client's blood calcium level, rather than any measure related to their bone mineral density","C":"Bone mineral density, providing a T-score used to diagnose osteoporosis and assess fracture risk","D":"The degree of inflammation present within a joint, rather than any measure related to bone density"}}
source_row.rationale: A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density, providing a T-score compared to young adult peak bone density, used to diagnose osteoporosis and assess fracture risk, the standard diagnostic tool for this condition.
source_row.source_name: National Osteoporosis Foundation — DEXA Scan Purpose
source_row.source_detail: Purpose and Interpretation of DEXA Scanning

source_row.stem: A provider uses the FRAX tool to assess a client's 10-year fracture risk. This tool incorporates:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly few established clinical inputs of any kind, relying instead mainly on rough guesswork by the treating provider","B":"Bone density alone, without factoring in any of the client's other individual clinical risk factors that might be present","C":"Just the results of genetic testing alone, rather than the broader set of clinical factors this tool actually incorporates into its final calculation","D":"Multiple clinical risk factors, such as age, prior fracture history, and certain medication use, along with bone density if available, to estimate fracture risk"}}
source_row.rationale: The FRAX tool incorporates multiple clinical risk factors, such as age, prior fracture history, and certain medication use (such as chronic corticosteroids), along with bone density if available, to provide a more comprehensive 10-year fracture risk estimate than bone density alone.
source_row.source_name: National Osteoporosis Foundation — FRAX Tool Use
source_row.source_detail: Components of FRAX Fracture Risk Assessment

source_row.stem: A nurse reviews serum calcium and phosphorus levels for a client with a significant fracture undergoing extensive bone healing. These levels are monitored because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Calcium and phosphorus are essential components of bone mineralization, and significant abnormalities could affect the healing process","B":"Fairly little ongoing monitoring actually being needed for these particular values during the course of fracture healing","C":"Bone healing being considered to carry fairly little relationship to the body's overall mineral metabolism","D":"Carrying fairly little established relationship at all to how bone tissue metabolizes and heals over time"}}
source_row.rationale: Calcium and phosphorus are essential components of bone mineralization, and monitoring these levels during significant fracture healing helps ensure adequate mineral availability to support the bone healing process, particularly relevant in clients with underlying metabolic bone conditions.
source_row.source_name: Standard Orthopedic References — Mineral Monitoring in Fracture Healing
source_row.source_detail: Role of Calcium/Phosphorus in Bone Healing

source_row.stem: A provider orders rheumatoid factor testing for a client with suspected rheumatoid arthritis. The nurse should understand that:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A positive result supports the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical context, but this test has limitations in both sensitivity and specificity","B":"A positive result definitively confirming a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis in essentially every client who tests positive","C":"A negative result definitively ruling out rheumatoid arthritis as a possible diagnosis for any given client","D":"This particular test carrying fairly little established role in the overall clinical evaluation of rheumatoid arthritis"}}
source_row.rationale: A positive rheumatoid factor result supports a rheumatoid arthritis diagnosis in the appropriate clinical context, but this test has limitations in both sensitivity (not all RA clients test positive) and specificity (the factor can be positive in other conditions or even healthy individuals), requiring correlation with clinical findings and often additional testing.
source_row.source_name: American College of Rheumatology — Rheumatoid Factor Testing Limitations
source_row.source_detail: Sensitivity and Specificity Limitations of RF Testing

source_row.stem: A nurse reviews a client's elevated ESR and CRP as part of evaluation for suspected inflammatory joint disease. These markers help:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Diagnosing one specific joint condition with full certainty, based on these two inflammatory markers alone without further testing","B":"Indicate the presence of systemic inflammation, supporting further evaluation, though these markers are nonspecific and require clinical correlation","C":"Carrying fairly little established relationship to inflammatory conditions despite being routinely checked for this exact reason","D":"Taking the place of any other diagnostic testing the provider would otherwise still need to order for the client"}}
source_row.rationale: Elevated ESR and CRP indicate the presence of systemic inflammation, supporting further evaluation for conditions like inflammatory arthritis, though these markers are nonspecific (elevated in many conditions) and require clinical correlation with other findings and testing rather than providing a definitive diagnosis alone.
source_row.source_name: American College of Rheumatology — Inflammatory Marker Use in Joint Disease
source_row.source_detail: Role and Limitations of ESR/CRP in Joint Evaluation

source_row.stem: A nurse assists with joint aspiration for a client with suspected osteoarthritis, distinguishing this from an inflammatory or septic process. Osteoarthritis synovial fluid is typically characterized by:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A high white blood cell count with a predominance of neutrophils, a pattern more consistent with septic arthritis","B":"Fluid that offers fairly little diagnostic value despite being a routine part of the joint aspiration workup","C":"Relatively clear fluid with a lower white blood cell count than seen in inflammatory or septic conditions","D":"Fluid with characteristics essentially identical to what would be seen in rheumatoid arthritis"}}
source_row.rationale: Osteoarthritis synovial fluid is typically characterized by relatively clear fluid with a lower white blood cell count than seen in inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or infectious conditions like septic arthritis, an important distinguishing feature in joint fluid analysis.
source_row.source_name: Clinical Rheumatology References — Synovial Fluid Analysis in Osteoarthritis
source_row.source_detail: Characteristic OA Synovial Fluid Findings

source_row.stem: A nurse teaches a client proper crutch walking technique following a lower extremity injury. Correct technique includes:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Using crutches that are sized identically for every client regardless of height","B":"Bearing weight through the hands on the crutch handgrips, not the axillae, to avoid nerve compression injury","C":"Bearing weight directly on the axillae for support, rather than through the hands as intended","D":"Fairly little specific weight-bearing technique consideration actually being needed with crutch use"}}
source_row.rationale: Proper crutch walking technique includes bearing weight through the hands on the crutch handgrips, not the axillae, since prolonged pressure on the axillae can cause nerve compression injury (sometimes called "crutch palsy"), along with proper crutch sizing individualized to the client's height.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Crutch Walking Technique Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Proper Weight-Bearing Technique with Crutches

source_row.stem: A nurse teaches a client with a new cast about home care. Key teaching points include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Keeping the cast dry, avoiding inserting objects inside to relieve itching, and elevating the extremity to reduce swelling","B":"Getting the cast wet not being considered much of a concern for the client to worry about","C":"Inserting objects inside the cast as an acceptable way to help relieve any itching the client experiences","D":"Fairly little specific home care teaching actually being needed for a client with a newly applied cast"}}
source_row.rationale: Cast care teaching includes keeping the cast dry (to prevent skin breakdown and material damage), avoiding inserting objects inside the cast to relieve itching (which can cause skin injury), and elevating the extremity to help reduce swelling, particularly important in the initial period after cast application.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Cast Care Patient Education Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Key Home Cast Care Teaching Points

source_row.stem: A nurse positions a client following total hip replacement surgery, using an abduction pillow between the legs. This positioning device helps:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Maintain proper hip positioning and reduce the risk of prosthetic dislocation during the immediate post-operative period","B":"Carrying fairly little established purpose in the care of a client recovering from hip replacement surgery","C":"Actually increasing the client's overall risk of experiencing a prosthetic dislocation during recovery","D":"Taking the place of the other movement precautions the client would otherwise still need to follow"}}
source_row.rationale: An abduction pillow placed between the legs after total hip replacement helps maintain proper hip positioning and reduce the risk of prosthetic dislocation during the immediate post-operative period, complementing (not replacing) other movement precautions taught to the client.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — Post-Hip Replacement Positioning Guidelines
source_row.source_detail: Purpose of Abduction Pillow Positioning

source_row.stem: A nurse assists a client with passive range of motion (ROM) exercises following orthopedic surgery, as prescribed. These exercises help:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Offering fairly little established benefit for a client's overall recovery following orthopedic surgery of this kind","B":"Help maintain joint mobility and prevent contractures, particularly important when a client cannot yet perform active exercises independently","C":"Taking the place of the physical therapy involvement the client would otherwise still need going forward with recovery","D":"Actually increasing the client's overall risk of developing a joint contracture over the course of their recovery"}}
source_row.rationale: Passive range of motion exercises help maintain joint mobility and prevent contractures, particularly important when a client cannot yet perform active exercises independently, an important nursing intervention that complements (not replaces) formal physical therapy involvement.
source_row.source_name: AAOS — ROM Exercise Guidelines in Orthopedic Recovery
source_row.source_detail: Purpose of Passive ROM Exercises

source_row.stem: A nurse counsels a client about weight-bearing exercise as part of osteoporosis prevention. This type of exercise is emphasized because:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Mainly non-weight-bearing exercise, such as swimming, being thought to provide meaningful benefits for a client's bone health","B":"Exercise recommendations being essentially identical, without much regard for an individual client's underlying bone health status or age","C":"Weight-bearing exercise helps stimulate bone formation and maintain bone density, an important modifiable factor in osteoporosis prevention","D":"Weight-bearing exercise carrying fairly little established relationship to a client's overall long-term bone health"}}
source_row.rationale: Weight-bearing exercise is emphasized in osteoporosis prevention because it helps stimulate bone formation and maintain bone density, an important modifiable factor, distinct from non-weight-bearing exercises like swimming, which offer cardiovascular benefits but less direct bone-loading stimulus.
source_row.source_name: National Osteoporosis Foundation — Exercise for Bone Health
source_row.source_detail: Weight-Bearing Exercise Benefits for Bone Density

source_row.stem: A nurse discusses fall prevention strategies with an older adult client to help reduce fracture risk. These strategies include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Restricting essentially all of the client's activity in an effort to eliminate their risk of falling entirely","B":"Home safety modifications, appropriate footwear, vision correction, and addressing any medications that may increase fall risk","C":"Strategies considered relevant mainly for clients who already have a documented history of a prior fall","D":"Fairly few established fall prevention strategies actually existing for nurses to discuss with older adult clients"}}
source_row.rationale: Fall prevention strategies for older adults include home safety modifications (such as removing tripping hazards), appropriate footwear, vision correction, and addressing any medications that may increase fall risk, proactive measures valuable for all older adults, not only those with a prior fall history.
source_row.source_name: CDC STEADI Initiative — Fall Prevention Strategies
source_row.source_detail: Comprehensive Fall Prevention Approach

source_row.stem: A nurse counsels a client about lifestyle factors that support bone health and help reduce fracture risk. These include:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Complete avoidance of essentially all physical activity as the primary recommended strategy for bone health","B":"Lifestyle factors being considered relevant mainly after a fracture has already occurred, rather than beforehand","C":"Fairly few established lifestyle factors actually having any meaningful influence on bone health or fracture risk","D":"Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake, regular weight-bearing exercise, and avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol intake"}}
source_row.rationale: Lifestyle factors supporting bone health and fracture risk reduction include adequate calcium and vitamin D intake, regular weight-bearing exercise, and avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol intake, proactive measures valuable throughout life, not only after a fracture has already occurred.
source_row.source_name: National Osteoporosis Foundation — Lifestyle Factors for Bone Health
source_row.source_detail: Comprehensive Bone Health Lifestyle Recommendations

source_row.stem: A nurse recognizes that a client with chronic musculoskeletal pain may experience significant psychological impact, including:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Anxiety, depression, and frustration related to the ongoing, often unpredictable nature of chronic pain, warranting recognition and appropriate support","B":"A condition generally considered unrelated to the client's overall quality of life on a day-to-day basis","C":"Fairly little meaningful psychological impact at all, since chronic pain is often assumed to be a purely physical experience for most people","D":"Psychological considerations being relevant mainly for pain related specifically to a cancer diagnosis, rather than other causes"}}
source_row.rationale: Chronic musculoskeletal pain can have significant psychological impact, including anxiety, depression, and frustration related to the ongoing, often unpredictable nature of the pain experience, warranting nursing recognition and appropriate support or referral, applicable across the range of chronic pain conditions, not only cancer-related pain.
source_row.source_name: Standard Pain Management References — Psychological Impact of Chronic Pain
source_row.source_detail: Recognizing Psychological Impact of Chronic Pain

source_row.stem: A nurse supports a client's psychological adjustment following limb amputation, recognizing potential body image concerns. This support includes:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Acknowledging the significant body image adjustment involved, providing emotional support, and connecting the client with resources such as peer support or counseling","B":"Avoiding any discussion of the client's own feelings about the amputation throughout the entire course of their recovery process at the facility","C":"Assuming that every client experiences essentially identical body image concerns following a limb amputation procedure of this particular kind","D":"Assuming that body image carries fairly little relevance to how well the client ultimately goes on to recover functionally"}}
source_row.rationale: Supporting a client's psychological adjustment after limb amputation includes acknowledging the significant body image adjustment involved, providing emotional support, and connecting the client with resources such as peer support or counseling, individualized to their specific experience and needs.
source_row.source_name: Amputee Coalition — Psychosocial Support After Amputation
source_row.source_detail: Body Image Considerations Following Amputation

source_row.stem: A nurse supports a client's psychological adjustment to a new, significant physical disability following an orthopedic injury. This adjustment process often includes:
source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly little need for any ongoing psychosocial support at all once the client's physical healing has been fully completed","B":"A range of emotional responses, potentially including grief, frustration, and gradual adaptation, similar to responses seen with other significant life changes","C":"Immediate, complete acceptance of the disability, without any real emotional adjustment period needed in the weeks and months afterward","D":"A process that unfolds in an essentially identical, fully predictable way for every single client who happens to experience it"}}
source_row.rationale: Psychological adjustment to a significant new physical disability often includes a range of emotional responses, potentially including grief, frustration, and gradual adaptation over time, similar to responses seen with other significant life changes, warranting individualized nursing support that continues beyond physical healing alone.
